extracted.intended_audience: university founders, administrators, educators, and students interested in the philosophy and design of higher education
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and standards for what a university should teach and what university education should aim to produce in students (the role of Theology, the unity of knowledge, liberal education, and limits of disciplinary claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality of a University (teach all sciences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whereas it is the very profession of a University to teach all sciences, on this account it cannot exclude Theology without being untrue to its profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A university should profess and provide instruction across the full circle of knowledge; excluding a branch (notably Theology) contradicts the institution's purpose and weakens the integrity of its teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of Theology among the Chairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Theology has a claim to be represented among the Chairs of a University.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theology completes and corrects other sciences, defends its own boundaries, and prevents adjacent sciences from usurping its province; omitting Theology invites other disciplines to teach, without warrant, conclusions on theological matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain proper boundaries between sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Each science has a proper province and must not overstep by pronouncing on matters which belong to another science (e.g., Political Economy pronouncing on spiritual beings; Comparative Anatomy declaring about immaterial soul).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate disciplines by whether they limit themselves to their premisses and methods. Guard against specialists treating their science as the final arbiter on questions outside its remit; require appeal to a higher or proper science where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exclusiveness and ‘making one’s own science the measure of all things’
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusive devotion to one science, treating it as the centre of all truth, leads to unconscious or conscious anti-religious conclusions and to scattering principles of one domain under the garb of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discourage curricula and practitioners that isolate a single discipline and let it monopolize interpretation of other domains; encourage awareness of the limits of disciplinary vantage points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against Private Judgment usurping other sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: When a science assumes certain principles as true without authority or appeal to a higher science, it is acting by Private Judgment and may infect other sciences with hostility to Theology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims for whether they rest only upon a discipline’s internal premisses or whether they invoke higher/authoritative grounds; critiques should call out unwarranted assertions (examples: Antiquarian saying everything must be in documents; Philosophic Historian assimilating Judaism to political institutions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the limits of disciplinary claims (sciences give hypothetical conclusions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sciences draw conclusions from their premisses and cannot legitimately declare ultimate ends or ethical truths (e.g., Political Economy can show how wealth is produced given that wealth is sought, but not that wealth ought to be sought as the summum bonum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require distinction between 'if' statements of a discipline (conditional advice) and unconditional ethical or theological claims; curricula and lecturers should avoid presenting hypothetical disciplinary results as final moral prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberal education: Knowledge as its own end
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge is capable of being its own end; University education should teach liberal or philosophical knowledge that is pursued for its own sake, not only for utilitarian ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value and assess programmes by whether they cultivate a comprehensive view of truth and the relations among sciences, and whether they present learning as intrinsically rewarding rather than solely instrumental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of a philosophical habit of mind in students
rubrics_metrics.description: A University’s education should form a habit of mind in students whose attributes are freedom, equitableness, calmness, moderation, and wisdom (a 'philosophical habit').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate teaching by its success in producing these character attributes rather than merely technical proficiency; promote breadth of study so students apprehend 'great outlines of knowledge' and learn to estimate values of different sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create an interdisciplinary, collegial intellectual atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: An assemblage of learned men, zealous for their own sciences and rivals of each other, brought together by intimate intercourse, adjust claims, learn to respect and aid each other, producing an 'intellectual tradition' that benefits students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess institutional design and practices for opportunities for interdepartmental consultation, mutual adjustment of claims, and a culture that exposes students to multiple sciences and perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance pursuit of knowledge with public duties and practical life
rubrics_metrics.description: The pursuit of knowledge must not carry one off from public occupations; acquiring knowledge should not be pursued so as to interfere with duties to family, society, and public life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design curricula and expectations so that students can pursue intellectual development without neglecting civic and practical responsibilities; recognize Cicero’s distinction that search after truth follows satisfaction of physical and political needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical/documentary evidence within its place (do not make it sole arbiter of religious truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: History and documentary testimony are invaluable but must not be assumed to be the sole means of gaining Religious Truth; overvaluing historical documents can illegitimately displace other modes of theological knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing historical-critical claims, require awareness of the limits of documentary silence and evidence (examples cited: Gibbon’s appeal to silence about the darkness at the Passion; Protestant and Arian uses of Fathers’ writings).
